newsitem.title: UK: Britain to fund research into deadly E coli.
newsitem.headline: Britain to fund research into deadly E coli.

text.p: The British government said on Wednesday it would back urgent research into the E coli food poisoning bug that killed 16 elderly people in Scotland in November and December.
Scottish Secretary Michael Forsyth said he accepted the recommendations made in a report by Hugh Pennington, an expert at Aberdeen University on E coli.

"This has been an extremely serious and tragic outbreak, one of the worst of its sort in the world," he told parliament. "This is a matter to which the government will attach the utmost priority in the coming months."
Forsyth said he had asked officials to examine urgently the use of emergency powers to close stores or food processing plants to prevent or limit outbreaks.

Pennington's report also called for changes in food safety laws to allow more careful licensing of food premises and said there should be better communication among government agencies and quicker ways to analyse the situation and provide information.

More than 400 people were treated for food poisoning in the two Scottish outbreaks in November and December. Sixteen victims, all elderly, died. Scottish butcher John Barr faces charges of culpable and reckless conduct in the case.

E coli is a normal digestive bacteria but one strain, known as 0157, can cause kidney failure and brain damage. It gets into the food supply through the use of manure and improper slaughtering techniques.
The deadliest outbreak was in Canada in 1985 when 19 elderly people died.
"It is much more virulent than most other causes of food poisoning and requires a smaller infective dose than other organisms such as salmonella," Forsyth said.
He said he had recommended urgent action on Pennington's proposal for scientists to find out how common E coli is in livestock and to seek better ways to identify it genetically.

George Robertson, Scottish spokesman for the opposition Labour Party, accused the government of doing too little, too late in the case. "(They) ignore medical advice (and) react to events rather than shape them," he told parliament.
